title: Inside Look: AI & Developer Productivity Programs in a 1,500+ Engineering Team

segments.text: I come back to the tech leader stage and to the next fireside chat. I'm really looking forward to that. It's really an on topic which comes right in time for
everything we're doing. We will talk about from AI adoption to what does it mean to be developer productivity. And there there's a special perception cuz
we have two of them. We will have on the customer side as well as the DX side. So therefore really we will talk about
what is productivity bringing, what are the platform behind, and therefore I'm really happy to really welcome here on stage Christian from Arrive as well as
Alan from DX and Atlassian plant. So please join me to welcome Alan Christian. Please come on stage. >> Okay. >> And the last point just for everybody
here, please take the opportunity in the app to really ask question. We will take these questions later to the Atlassian booth which is just behind you. And with
that, up to you Alan and Christian. Have fun. >> Thank you. >> Thank you. >> Thank you guys for coming. Um, as mentioned, I'm Ellen Jones. I'm a
customer success leader at DX, one of the Atlassian brands, and I'm joined here by one of our fantastic customers, Christian from the Arrive team.
Christian, I'll let you introduce yourself briefly. >> Yeah, hi. Uh, I'm Christian and I'm um, responsible for developer experience, platform foundations, and AI adoption at
Arrive. And Arrive is a global mobility platform that represents brands like RingGo, EasyPark Parkmobile Flowbird. >> So let's dive in. Um, today we really
want to hear from Christian about their AI adoption journey and how far they've come in that journey. So, Christian, let's start with with your rollout. For
an org your size, a massive enterprise org, how did you manage to achieve about 95% adoption so quickly? How did you structure that? How did you accomplish
that? >> Uh yeah, so our AI journey actually started in uh 2025 in uh in summer. So, since we are customers of Microsoft, Copilot was just there for us. And uh
that's where we decided we are going with GitHub Copilot. And actually when we rolled out the licenses, we thought that let's start with the workshops right
away because from previous experience, I knew that rolling out new tools is uh quite difficult and the adoption takes really some effort. And we started with
workshops right away. We did uh tens of workshops and during 2025, we reached to a 50% of adoption rate. Then early this year, 2026,
we rolled out Claude Code. And uh I would say that's where things really took off. >> Mhm. >> Uh within the first 24 hours after me
announcing in our Slack channel, "Hey, Claude Code is now available. Whoever is interested, go go and have it." We had around 400 engineers using it
right away just in 24 hours. And in 1 month, we had 800 weekly active users. So, it really took off and I haven't seen such
high adoption rate uh in our organization like anywhere. Uh but I mean, the journey from 57% to 95, it wasn't like four or five-month miracle. So,
uh first of we had this Copilot foundation uh from previous year and Cloud Code was accelerating on top of it. And we also, what we decided is, um,
we need to do the training org-wide. So, what we did, we did over 30 sessions in nine countries and we trained over 1,200 tech and
product people. So, it was two-day in-person hands-on hackathon where we gathered engineers and product people and we teach them how models actually work, how
to use them and after that everyone was running their own agents. So, that's the bit what we did. >> And those sessions were required. They
were not just an optional come if you'd like to learn more. This was a requirement of the org to set that expectation that you had to learn how to
use the tooling and get everyone involved in in the hype. Um, Christian, I do hear from a lot of customers that maybe they have a a split
developer team in terms of some developers are really eager and excited to use the tools and some are maybe more hesitant or are more skeptical of the
quality that's going to come out of these tools. So, did you experience that? Did you have developers that had skepticism and maybe how did you
approach that and get everyone really on board? >> Yeah. So, I mean, that's totally normal. We all we have like everyone in our organization, we have like skeptics and
in a size like ours, so there are there those people. Um, what I could say like what was the turning point? So, I'm not
a believer in enforcement. We didn't do any like messaging, uh, to turn them like around to use those tools. I think what helped was having them for
those two days in the room with others where they could actually see how it works. And this is what was the turning point that changed their opinion.
And yeah, I think the skepticism turned into curiosity and curiosity turned into excitement. And that's what the training was all about, I would say.
>> I think that's a missing piece that I just hear across the customer base is a lot of companies not investing in building that hype and building that
excitement and building those cohorts internally and those feedback loops and that collaboration. We see cross-team collaboration declining sometimes as AI tools are increasing adoption and we
want to avoid that and I think that's something really incredible that you've managed to do within your org in order to keep that collaboration
going and keep everyone really excited about the usage. Um so I want to pivot a little bit. I want to shift now into really like the next phase of this and
and that comes down to tracking. How are you defining adoption? How are you tracking adoption? How are you defining and tracking impact? Let's talk a little
bit more about those pieces and kind of that next phase. >> Um so the basic question whether people are using it um turned not so interesting to us anymore. So we
are basically saturated. We have reached the the adoption. So what is now interesting is the intensity or the depth. So how deeply people are using it.
Weekly active user users, daily active usage. And as of right now, we have 86% of engineers who are using AI tools daily. And more than half of our
um uh half of our code that we build and ship is written by AI. So um that's about adoption. So regarding impact I mean, basic stuff. We are looking at
PR throughput. >> Mhm. >> Uh during this year, we are up about 30%. >> Mhm. >> Also, the PRs themselves have gotten bigger. >> Mhm.
>> Like, two times bigger. So, each PR now uh has more work in it. And uh cycle time. So, yeah, this has increased as well by
uh 30%. >> Mhm. >> I would say it's not a bottleneck for us right now, but it's definitely something we need to keep an eye on because review
like, yeah, we see engineers are becoming more uh reviewers. So, this is something yeah, I'm looking at. Also, cost per PR is what I'm interested
in. So, this metric varies a lot from team to team. And all in all, I would say um we treat all of those system metrics
as learning points for teams. We don't rank teams against each other or compare. So um yeah, just wanted to mention that as well. So, the only fair comparison is
team against its own trend. So, that's uh that's yeah, in my opinion. Uh the other thing I'm especially interested right now is allocation or innovation ratio.
It turns out that uh the more we build, the more we have to maintain. And the majority of the work that we do is
maintenance and fixes rather than new features. So, we have become more efficient. The throughput numbers prove it, but we also have created more maintenance. That's what I call the
maintenance paradox. So, how do we use the same AI leverage that we are getting uh in throughput to tackle maintenance burden at scale. So, this is the question I'm personally

struggling with my team right now. And uh yeah, we have started offloading maintenance work to background agents. For example, fixing critical vulnerabilities CVs doing version upgrades, or large-scale
code base migrations. So, those are like quite good candidates for background agents. And we call it fleet management. But, this is I believe some of you might have heard
this from Spotify as well. They are calling it fleet shift, and their background agents are called Honk. I think Stripe is doing something similar as well. They call it
Minions. So, this isn't anything new. Companies are already doing this. Um but, yeah, the main goal is to take away the maintenance burden from product
teams. So, they could um create more features, and focus on creating the value more value for the customers. >> Yeah. >> So, that's the goal.
>> I think it's so important for everyone to remember that while we're utilizing AI as an accelerator, it is it will generate potentially new
bottlenecks, and that's very inevitable. Um and some of those new bottlenecks can be on that maintenance side. Um we're now the results, the aftermath is a
whole new infrastructure that's larger, more complex, and needs to be maintained. And I love that you're tackling that with AI. You know, the aftermath of using AI as an accelerator,
you're also using AI to solve those new bottlenecks. So, I just think it's a really cool approach. You also touched on something about not comparing teams
against each other. Um and I think that's really interesting. I I um across the customer base kind of a controversial topic when it comes to team comparisons and the the
reality is all of you know, it's not apples to apples. Teams all operate very differently. Their adoption rates or their impact will be very different. And
I think it is important to keep that in mind as we're comparing teams against each other. It's not always the best the best way to be looking at the data.
Those trend lines are the most impactful piece. Are you trending in the right direction? >> Mhm. Yeah. >> So, I want to talk a little bit
about the the system metrics. So, you mentioned some of these system metrics that you're tracking. Feels very organic to track throughput, cycle time, review
turnaround time. All of these systematic metrics that we can be looking at. How are you also leveraging self-reported data and how you know, you built this
great community internally where there's these feedback loops and there's a lot of collaboration. How are you ingesting that data and then what are you finding from the self-reported
data? >> Uh so, the system data usually tells you what's happening in the system. But it doesn't tell you why. >> Mhm. >> So, that's why we are doing quarterly
developer experience surveys >> Mhm. >> uh among our engineers. And this has been quite popular, I would say. The lowest adoption rate that we have
seen is 95%. So, and our developers are quite engaged and they are quite vocal about different areas. So, the idea is to find how developers feel. So, where they are
feeling and seeing friction. So, system data doesn't reveal that. It just so shows you whether I don't know PR throughput throughput is up or down or
cycle time, whatever. But what is the actual problem? What's causing this? So, I think this is um really interesting to see. Um We just finished our snapshot a week
ago. And we uh received about 700 comments from engineers. And I think the most popular topics for our engineers were the most vocal were
testing and pipelines, documentation, prioritization planning. I mean, those are all process-related. It It's like about AI tooling, we we simply didn't receive any feedback at
all. So, I would say the next gains in our organization are related to organizational processes, not buying another AI tool. >> Mhm. >> So, um yeah.
>> Are you going to be leveraging AI to resolve any of those organizational and process bottlenecks? >> Uh yeah, absolutely. I mean, since testing came up,
we are struggling in some areas with test coverage. This is probably one of the areas we will look into. Review is definitely the other one. How
do we make review smoother? How do we take this review review toil from engineers? So, absolutely, yeah. >> Yeah. >> Also, documentation. >> Yeah. Yeah. Are you Talk to me. Okay, so
we've been very focused on the engineering side. How is this How are you thinking about AI more widely spread across the org? Product teams, design
teams, is that something that's top of mind for you? How are you approaching that? >> Yes. So, when I wrote that Cloud Code is
now available, I wrote that in technic technology channel. But 20% of our user base using Cloud Code is non-technical. So, yeah, I mean, right after we did uh this org-wide
Cloud training, we thought to ourselves like like why would we stop training engineers? Why not take this to org-wide? So, we launched the AI Academy
where you will be taken to a 6-week journey and you all the uh like uh training content is curriculum-based. So, whether you're sales, HR,
operations, marketing, you will get your personalized curriculum. And this has been quite successful uh for us, I would say, because we have uh onboarded nearly 2,000 people already
and we have uh 1. 3K active weekly users. So, it has been quite popular and uh yeah. >> That investment in the education that
you're providing, I I mean, I would love to do a full ROI on, you know, how much time you invested into putting together that education and then what that has
given you in return. And especially in regards to these fringe teams that are not as technical and maybe don't as easily adopt and learn how to use these
tools. That is so incredibly important that you're doing that and you're making them feel feel really comfortable. Um I think speaking of like tracking and
and ROI, how are you guys reporting this upwards to leadership and and maybe I'm going to ask you three questions in one, you know, where is the ownership of this
tracking and reporting living? Are EMs responsible for tracking the adoption and impact of their own teams? Um is that something you personally have to do
just across the whole org yourself? You know, how how are you reporting this upwards and and what's the responsibility at that EM level? >> For senior leadership, um so far, I've
done monthly reports and I try to cover three aspects. AI cost, AI adoption, and productivity. So, I use those dimensions to tell a data-driven story and being truly
honest. So, there are the areas where we are doing well and the areas where we are lacking behind or where are the biggest uh
uh obstacles. And that has been worked quite well for us, I would say. Um yeah, that's that's that's how we have looked at this. Also,
one interesting thing, I don't know how about you, but I've never seen our CFO being so interested in developer productivity than right now. >> [laughter]
>> I wonder why that is. >> Are you reporting like cost management and token usage? Kind of what kind of financial data are you providing to to
the CFO? >> Uh yeah, I'm touching cost aspects as well. So, how are we using what models are we using and so on. And it And I try to combine
those different aspects and correlate to some sort of a correlation to craft a story because you can't uh like focus on one aspect. You have to
look it from different angles. And even from productivity point of view, you can't just simply look at PR throughput and say that whether this is good or bad. You have to
look at from different angles and that's what I try to do uh here as well and report it to senior uh leadership. >> When you think about um
capacity and um like headcount planning, capacity planning, are EMs now going to be planning not just for the physical headcount of developers on their team,
but also planning for the cost of bringing more agents and more AI tooling into their orgs? Is that going to be a part of forecasting within management?
>> Um right now, I think for us it's mainly about central visibility. We have dashboards in place that shows tool usage, that shows adoption, uh
etc. But yeah, as you mentioned, the goal where we are after at is since the EM already owns the head count decision, um yeah, the the financials
team-wise, so I think the natural step is for them to own AI cost as well. So in that way they can make the trade-off
decisions between head count and AI budget. >> Mhm. >> And I mean, I think in the future EMs should predict how much token usage they
are going to need. I mean, every team is different. They have different missions, they have different dynamics. Like there is no way that we can look at whatever
dashboard or central metric to say that this team needs that and the other ones diff Yeah, it's quite difficult. Uh the other one is outcome. So what is
the outcome that team produces? I think manager and the team, they are the closest one to actually know whether the outcome is good or bad.
>> Mhm. >> And yeah, that's why it makes natural that the team makes this decision and whether we should increase the AI budget or not.
>> Yeah. >> So >> That makes a lot of sense. >> Are the Jira backlogs getting thinner or not? I mean, >> Yeah. So let's see here. As we we wrap up, I
know a lot of you likely have a lot of questions and we Christian and I are actually going to be migrating just over to the Atlassian
booth here in a moment, doing a little bit of a deeper dive into how DX can actually help track all of this. You know, Christian mentioned some of the
self-reported data that they're gathering and that's something that they're leveraging DX for. We'd love to really dive into those mechanics and how you can be leveraging that to to track
all of this. Um you know, you've shared a lot of really great information. And again, I I talked to being a customer success leader, I
talked to so many customers that are struggling with these problems. And and I can just tell they're begging for help. They're begging for advice. And
you're sharing a lot of good advice here. If everyone in this room had to walk away learning maybe three main things, you know, what would you love
for them to walk away knowing? >> So, I'm speaking what we have done. So, the first one is invest into people. We have a
made a deliberate bet to invest into training. And yeah, we have seen quite good results. Because the technology space is evolving so rapidly. So, we have decided we are
going to invest in our people, train them, and engineers know how to use those tools, etc. What is the best use case? So, yeah, this is the first one.
Invest in people and in training. The second one what we have done is um we have champions in each hub. So, of course, we have those early
adopters that are really excited about new things. So, we should use them. And peers also always trust what they're um other peers vouch for. So, it's not like
top-down. Um We also did um many demos, not just like vendor-like demos, but actual teams presenting their actual work. For example, during all-hands presentation. So,
this has been also quite successful. And we have quite popular community. I think Cloud Code community is one of the popular ones in our Slack now. So,
there's a lot of going on there. Uh and I think the third one is everything around the data, the metrics, the sentiment data. I mean, you have to look at both sides.
Of course, we can't forget the system data, but we also have to look at sentiment data and see what is the friction in our system.
So, where our engineers actually feeling feeling stuck? Where is the flow being cut off for engineers? And I think combining those two has worked quite well for us. And I
mean, yeah, DX does quite quite good job in that sense. And by the way, I'm not I'm not getting paid for saying that. >> [gasps]
>> It's quite opposite, actually. >> [laughter] >> I think it's really incredible to just remember that it's just like rolling out anything else within your environment.
You know, developers need to be trained. They need to feel excited about it. They need to feel a sense of community about adopting something new into their
workflow and into their daily practice. Um, expectations need to be set around how to utilize this new tool or this new mechanism in their daily practice. And,
you know, seeing Arrive has not approached AI in any different way than they've approached anything else they would roll out within their org. And
maybe even approach this with more aggressive guidance than other things that you've rolled out is really cool. I hear from a lot of customers
that maybe that all they've done is purchase licenses and just make them available to developers and say, "We have a senior team. Everyone should just
be adopting this and using it really well and doubling throughput." And they're really jumping over this enablement step, which is so important and and very complex as as Christian has
outlined, but so important and such a strong investment. Um, so I love hearing everything that you guys are doing. This is so helpful. I hope it's been helpful
for for everybody here as well. Um, as I mentioned, I definitely would love for for guys to join us just across in the Atlassian booth probably about 15
minutes. We'll kick off a a lightning talk here a little bit more about these AI measurement frameworks, how you can actually put this into practice, and
some of the the fundamentals of tracking developer experience and productivity, and how those fundamentals really haven't changed um with with AI. We still want to be tracking these things
the same way with that AI um measurement layered on top. So, yeah, this has been awesome. Thank you, Christian. We appreciate you being here.
I dragged Christian all the way here kind of last minute, and he was so gracious to join us and and share his story. So, we appreciate everyone. Thank
you. >> [applause]
